title: Insurance giant says Vic car theft crisis is now built into its business model — and you’ll pay more
full_text:
Victoria’s status as the car and property theft capital of Australia has been built into the business model of the country’s biggest insurer which has warned is considers the lawlessness the “new normal”.
Insurance Australia Group, which ruled off a 24.8 per cent slide in its profits to $1.02bn on Thursday, warned customers they would continue to face price rises in the year ahead amid bullish growth plans.
But IAG chief executive Nick Hawkins said there were key factors driving price growth, among them theft and natural disaster.
Mr Hawkins said Victoria was at the centre of a rise in car theft and resultant insurance payouts.
“We are assuming that’s the new norm now until there’s evidence otherwise. That’s the actual experience we’re seeing,” he said.
IAG has been grappling with an explosion in the cost of insurance as well as natural disasters.
Last financial year the company paid $12.4bn in claims.
But Australia and New Zealand’s record run of natural catastrophes hit IAG’s results, outrunning its budget by $114m.
In total, IAG faced $1.57bn in claims for natural catastrophes in the year.
Next year, IAG said it expects to face claims of $1.49bn for natural perils.
Mr Hawkins said this number was made worse by IAG’s purchase of RACQ, with the insurer hammered by hail claims while not subject to reinsurance provided by IAG.
IAG, which writes the NRMA, RACV, CGU, and WFI brands, said its underlying insurance operation had performed well, delivering a $1.57bn profit.
Its premiums were up around 5 per cent, hitting $18.4bn.
IAG told investors it planned to grow its insurance business by a further 5-8 per cent in the year ahead. It aims to have 11 million customers by 2030.
Mr Hawkins said Australians continued to purchase insurance, but noted some had responded to a cost-of-living crunch by lifting excesses, the money required to be paid before insurance could kick in. He said this was particularly so in property.
But Mr Hawkins said this would benefit only IAG, as smaller insurance claims were “harder to manage”.
“That’s a positive in our view, as people are confident with what they’re covering,” he said.
Some customers were also responding by dropping the level of insurance coverage on second cars.
Mr Hawkins said the insurance industry needed an answer to customers facing increasingly unaffordable cover.
“We don’t want people dropping out,” he said.
“We don’t want this to happen, this is not good for the country.”
IAG declared a 20c final dividend, taking full-year returns to 32c, up 1c on 2025 levels.
